subtype: Approach: rebuild with documents, insurance and mental-health support [Revision]
passage:
Day 4. At a desk in the relief camp, Gopika filled in the forms for flood assistance while the clerk stamped each page. Her ID card and mark sheets had gone brown in the water, so she also listed them as lost.

Day 12. Thomas, the insurance agent from the bank, sat with her while she attached photos of the waterline on the walls and of the ruined books to the claim. She also wrote to the college for duplicate papers.

Day 30. Gopika had been waking at night, listening for water that was not there. She noticed it was not getting better on its own. On Monday she booked a weekly slot with the college counsellor and wrote it in the same notebook as her list of papers.

qa.q: What did Gopika attach to the insurance claim?
qa.a: She attached photos of the waterline on the walls and of the ruined books.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling on Day 30 when she woke at night?
qa.a: Gopika was frightened and worn down, realising that the nights were not getting better on their own.

qa.q: What else could help Gopika's recovery, and why?
qa.a: Gopika could keep a folder of every receipt and reply and lean on friends for the tiring parts, because recovery has many small steps and sharing them lightens the load.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Gopika's way of going about it?
qa.a: Thomas would probably feel that a claim with photos and forms in order is easier to process, and might feel some relief at working with someone so organised.

grounding: Illustrates a person applying for relief, filing an insurance claim with photos, replacing lost papers and seeing a counsellor, in stages after a disaster.

subtype: Approach: rehearse an earthquake drill at home [Thinking]
passage:
Deepak: So you turned the living room into a drill ground?

Sumit: Kind of! My thinking was simple. In a real shake I won't have time to think, so my body has to already know. I chose the dining table because the legs are thick and it's away from the glass cabinet. Then I checked the two ways out, the front door and the service stairs, and made sure nothing was stacked in front of them. Drop, cover, hold on: down on my knees, under the table, one hand on a leg. My younger brother and sister thought it was a game, so I let them time each other. We did it three Sundays in a row. The third time neither of them asked why any more, they just dropped.

qa.q: Which piece of furniture did Sumit choose for cover?
qa.a: Sumit chose the dining table.

qa.q: What did Sumit believe about how the body reacts in a real earthquake?
qa.a: Sumit believed there would be no time to think, so the body has to already know what to do, which shows a wish to feel ready rather than helpless.

qa.q: What could Sumit add to make the drill stronger, and why?
qa.a: Sumit could practise at a different time or in the dark, because a real shake will not wait for a convenient moment.

qa.q: How might Sumit's younger brother see the drill?
qa.a: Sumit's younger brother probably saw it as a game at first, then felt safer as it became automatic.

grounding: Illustrates practising drop, cover and hold on at home, choosing a sturdy table and exits and teaching younger siblings, so panic becomes a learned response.

subtype: Approach: ration supplies and check on stranded relatives [Revision]
passage: By the second morning the corridor floor of the hostel was under an inch of water and the mess had shut. Hrithik went from room to room on the third floor and counted: nine packets of biscuits, two bags of puffed rice, a tin of tea leaves and twenty-two bottles of water among fourteen students. He had eaten a big breakfast as usual, and now the numbers made his stomach tighten. "We planned as if it was one day," he told Avni from the next room. Together they rewrote it: three small meals, water in cups, and a chart taped to the door. Then they tried every way of reaching home. The hostel landline crackled, texts kept failing, and near midnight one finally went through to Hrithik's cousin in the next district.

qa.q: How many bottles of water did Hrithik count?
qa.a: Hrithik counted twenty-two bottles of water among fourteen students.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling as he counted the supplies?
qa.a: Hrithik felt anxious, his stomach tightening as he realised the plan had been for one day.

qa.q: What else could the group do to stretch supplies, and why?
qa.a: They could ask the other floors and the warden about their stock and plan together, because a shared count shows how long everything must last.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt as the plan came together?
qa.a: Avni probably felt relieved to have a clear plan and stayed worried until a message finally got through.

grounding: Illustrates a person trapped by floods counting food and water, replanning consumption around the limit, and trying every channel to reach relatives.

subtype: Approach: notice the warning signs of pressure and isolation [Thinking]
passage: Ganga's invitation had sounded harmless: tea, laughter, a "growth circle" on Sunday afternoons. By the third session Bhavna noticed what she had been too flattered to see. The leader said family drained a person's energy, so calls home could wait. A fee of forty thousand rupees would "unlock the next level", due by Friday, right in her exam week. Anyone who asked a question was called weak. In the corridor she tried out the thoughts silently. Why is my mother a problem? Why is there a deadline? Why is asking a weakness? Three signals, one pattern. "I need to think, not decide," she told Ganga, and left before the closing chant. That night she called home for the first time in nine days.

qa.q: What fee did the leader ask for, and by when?
qa.a: The leader asked for a fee of forty thousand rupees, due by Friday.

qa.q: What made Bhavna uneasy?
qa.a: Bhavna grew uneasy because the leader discouraged calls home, pressed for money by a deadline and called questioners weak.

qa.q: What else could Bhavna do to test the group, and why?
qa.a: Bhavna could talk it over with family or a friend and look for independent information, because outside views help check what a closed group says.

qa.q: How might Ganga see Bhavna leaving early?
qa.a: Ganga may feel hurt or worried, believing the circle is good and taking the early exit as a rejection.

grounding: Illustrates noticing pressure, isolation from family and payment demands from a friendly self-improvement group, which creates distance.

subtype: Approach: keep outside relationships and reality checks [Action]
passage:
Avni: Everyone says you were the only one who walked out. How?

Yamini: Honestly, I didn't walk out at first. What helped was that I kept ordinary things going. Every Sunday I still called home, and I still had dinner with my old roommate on Wednesdays. After each meeting I told them what the group had said. One night I repeated a line the leader liked, "doubt just means your ego is talking." My roommate laughed and said, "How convenient for whoever is saying it." I heard it from outside for the first time. The group kept telling me my family didn't understand me, but the calls sounded so normal, so unhurried, next to the meetings. That gap kept showing me what was off.

qa.q: How often did Yamini call home?
qa.a: Yamini called home every Sunday.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when the roommate laughed at the leader's line?
qa.a: Yamini was startled, then clearer: hearing the line from outside made it sound different.

qa.q: What else could Yamini do to keep a clear view, and why?
qa.a: Yamini could write down what the group asks for and compare it with what family and friends think, because a written record is harder to explain away.

qa.q: How might the roommate have felt hearing Yamini's updates?
qa.a: The roommate probably felt worried but glad to be trusted, and helped just by listening and asking plain questions.

grounding: Illustrates keeping weekly calls with family and old friends and discussing the group's claims with them, so outside views break the closed loop.

subtype: Approach: commit gradually because each step seemed small [Pitfall]
passage: You asked why I never say "just try one session", Devika. Let me tell you. I'm Ishita. I was twenty. A classmate invited me to a free workshop on confidence, and it was lovely. The next month there was a small donation for the hall. Then a larger one for study materials. Then the group needed me on weekdays, and I told myself college could wait a semester. Each step felt like only a little more than the last, so I never saw the staircase I was climbing. The day my mother came to the group's house and asked me to walk home, I stood there and could not explain how I had got there. It took me a year to leave, and my savings never came back.

qa.q: What was the first thing the classmate offered Ishita?
qa.a: The classmate offered a free workshop on confidence.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when the mother asked to walk home?
qa.a: Ishita felt stuck and embarrassed, unable to explain how things had gone so far.

qa.q: At which point in the story could Ishita have stopped, and why?
qa.a: Ishita could have stopped at the first donation, when a free workshop turned into a request for money, because that was the earliest clear change.

qa.q: How did Ishita's mother see the situation at the group's house?
qa.a: Ishita's mother was probably frightened and heartbroken, standing in a stranger's house and asking Ishita to come home.

grounding: Illustrates joining a group through small steps, from a free workshop to donations and leaving college, where each step seemed consistent with the last.

subtype: Approach: set limits on time and money in advance [Action]
passage:
Thursday night. Vaibhav has asked me to a seminar on Saturday, and something in me says go carefully. So I sat down with my notebook and wrote three rules before I go. One: two hours at most, then I leave, whatever is happening. Two: no money, not even a "refundable deposit". Three: nothing signed on the spot. If there's a form, I take a photo and read it at home. I read the rules to Vaibhav on the phone. There was a sigh, but a fine at the end of it. I've set a phone reminder for four o'clock to leave. The rules feel a bit silly and also a bit like a seatbelt. I'll write again after Saturday.

Sharmila

qa.q: How long does Sharmila plan to stay at the seminar?
qa.a: Sharmila plans to stay two hours at most.

qa.q: How does Sharmila feel about the three rules?
qa.a: Sharmila feels they are a bit silly but also protective, like a seatbelt.

qa.q: What else could Sharmila do, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila could tell a trusted friend the plan and the leaving time so someone can check in, because limits are easier to keep when another person knows them.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel on hearing the rules?
qa.a: Vaibhav may feel a little hurt or irritated at being treated with caution, which fits the sigh, though the answer was still fine.

grounding: Illustrates setting limits on time, money and signing before attending a group event, so the limits are harder to wear down in the moment.

subtype: Approach: ask for details and independent information [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday. Swati took me to the wellness circle again, and this time I made myself ask. Where does the monthly contribution go? Who runs it? Why can't members see accounts? The leader smiled and said, "Trust is part of the journey." That is not an answer. Tonight I searched the group's name with the word "complaints" and found two news reports and a post by an ex-member who was told to cut off her sister. I showed Swati. Swati said they were just bitter people. Maybe. But a group that goes cold when you ask where the money goes doesn't feel healthy to me. I'm not going on Thursday. Not deciding forever, only this week.

Dilnaz

qa.q: Which questions did Dilnaz ask the leader?
qa.a: Dilnaz asked where the monthly contribution goes, who runs the circle and why members can't see accounts.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz think of the leader's reply?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt uneasy and unsatisfied, because "Trust is part of the journey" did not answer anything.

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz do to understand the group, and why?
qa.a: Dilnaz could talk it over with a family member or a college counsellor and read more accounts from former members, because outside experience helps check the group's own story.

qa.q: How might Swati feel about Dilnaz's decision not to go?
qa.a: Swati might feel defensive and hurt, having brought Dilnaz along and believing the circle has been good for others.

grounding: Illustrates asking where funds go, who leads and what former members say, and looking up independent information about a group.

subtype: Approach: give in to social pressure to belong [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday night. Eight weeks in Bengaluru and this is the first place that feels like home. Lakshmi hugged me at the door again and said, "We were waiting for you." Everyone here knows my name. Tonight the leader said people who keep "checking" are scared of being happy. I had a question about the retreat payment and I swallowed it. Maybe the doubt is my own problem, my old habit of not trusting good things. I signed up for the retreat and paid from my rent money. My school friend Meena called twice this week and I let it ring. I'll explain later. Right now it's easier to stay where I'm wanted.

Shalini

qa.q: What question did Shalini swallow tonight?
qa.a: Shalini swallowed a question about the retreat payment.

qa.q: What might Shalini be feeling when swallowing the question about the retreat payment?
qa.a: Shalini feels lonely and guilty, wanting so much to belong that the doubt is pushed down as a personal failing.

qa.q: What could Shalini do instead of staying quiet, and why?
qa.a: Shalini could ask the question aloud and keep in touch with people outside the group, because someone who welcomes questions is a safer sign than someone who calls them fear.

qa.q: How might Meena see Shalini's silence?
qa.a: Meena might feel worried and left out, calling twice and hearing nothing back from someone who used to answer.

grounding: Illustrates giving in to social pressure to belong in a new city, valuing the warm welcome and reading doubt as a personal failing.

subtype: Approach: step away with support and a safe exit plan [Revision]
passage: In a rented room in Leeds, Siddiq read the message again: "Come alone tomorrow, the leader wants a private word." His stomach tightened. For weeks the evening meetings had felt friendly, but the private talks had begun asking for his passport "for safekeeping". He called Valentina, a friend from his course. "I want to stop going. Will you be at my flat at six?" She said yes and told him to ring his parents as well. The next day he did not go. Two members waited outside his building, and Valentina and a flatmate stayed at his side until they left. He wrote to the group that he would not be back and saved every message. His parents told him that if anyone threatened him he should call the police.

qa.q: What had the private talks begun asking for?
qa.a: The private talks had begun asking for his passport for safekeeping.

qa.q: How was Siddiq feeling when he read the message?
qa.a: Siddiq felt uneasy and anxious, and his stomach tightened.

qa.q: What else could Siddiq do, and why?
qa.a: Siddiq could tell a course tutor or the university welfare team and go to the police if threats came, because more people who know make the exit safer.

qa.q: How might Valentina have seen the situation?
qa.a: Valentina was probably worried but glad to be trusted, and ready to stay by his side.

grounding: Illustrates stepping away from a group by telling a trusted friend, avoiding private meetings and leaning on family with the police as a fallback.
